A 54-year-old male was sent to the emergency department (ED) within 30 min of being found unresponsive at a health spa. His medical history was limited to treated hepatitis C and a remote appendectomy, with no known chronic illnesses or regular medication use. Upon arrival, his vital signs were notable for relative hypotension (104/58 mmHg), bradypnea (12 breaths/min), and hypothermia (34.3 °C), with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of E3V2M5. Physical examination revealed a state of flaccid paralysis with generalized areflexia, including absent deep tendon reflexes. Laboratory screening for common drugs of abuse was negative. message.content: metabolic acidosis with a pH of 7.28, a partial pressure of carbon dioxide of 52 mmHg, a serum bicarbonate of 16 mEq/L, and an elevated lactate of 4.2 mmol/L. Given the combination of unexplained coma, hypothermia, bradypnea, and flaccid areflexic paralysis, toxic ingestion was strongly suspected despite the negative initial screen. The patient was intubated for airway protection and started on empirical supportive therapy, including active rewarming with warmed intravenous fluids and a forced diuresis protocol. A collateral history obtained from a family member revealed that the patient had recently obtained botulinum toxin and colchicine through an online source for cosmetic purposes, raising concern for iatrogenic botulism. A serum sample was therefore sent for botulinum toxin testing, and the patient was treated empirically with heptavalent botulinum antitoxin. Over the following 48 hours, however, he failed to improve; pupils remained midposition and reactive, and repeat neurologic examinations continued to show profound flaccid weakness. Additional history from a coworker ultimately disclosed that the patient had been consuming an herbal preparation containing autumn crocus (Colchicum autumnale) leaves, which he had mistakenly foraged and brewed as a tea in the days preceding presentation. Colchicine toxicity was suspected, and this was later confirmed by measurement of a serum colchicine concentration of 12 ng/mL approximately 72 hours after ingestion. Supportive care was intensified with aggressive fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia, and monitoring for the anticipated hematologic complications. By hospital day 4, the patient developed leukopenia and thrombocytopenia consistent with colchicine's known suppression of bone marrow proliferation, along with a rising creatinine consistent...
